opus-5.5.text:
So in a standard Monte Carlo tree search for Go, every node is a board position, and each child is the position you get after making one particular move. The naive way to build that is as a strict tree: every path from the root gets its own copy of every node. But Go has a ton of transpositions. If I play A then you play B then I play C, that can land on exactly the same board as me playing C, you playing B, then me playing A. In a pure tree those show up as two completely separate nodes, each with its own visit counts and value estimates, even though they're literally the same position.

So when I say merging child nodes, I mean recognizing that two different branches have converged on an identical state, usually by hashing the board with something like Zobrist hashing, and collapsing them into a single node. That turns your tree into a directed acyclic graph. The payoff is that statistics are shared: any simulation that passes through that position, by any route, updates the same value estimate, so you get much more out of your search budget instead of re-evaluating the same position over and over with the neural net.

The subtlety, and why it's not totally trivial, is that in Go the board alone isn't quite the full state. You've got the ko rule and superko, which depend on history, and whose turn it is, and things like captured stones for scoring. So you have to be careful about what counts as "the same" node. And then backing up values gets trickier in a DAG, because a node now has multiple parents, and you have to decide how visit counts and Q-values propagate so you don't double count or end up with inconsistent statistics. There's some nice work on doing that cleanly, but conceptually the idea is simple: don't think about the same position twice just because you arrived at it in a different order.

r001.rationale: The response gives two different move orders—A-B-C and C-B-A—that reach exactly the same board position.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So if you think about how something like AlphaGo or MuZero does Monte Carlo tree search, you start from the current board position, that's your root node, and each child is a possible move. You expand the tree by simulating moves, backing up value estimates, and over time the visit counts concentrate on the branches that look promising.

The thing is, in Go a lot of different move sequences lead to the exact same board position. If I play A then B, and you play C then D, that can produce the same stones on the board as me playing B then A and you playing D then C. Move order doesn't always matter. So in a naive tree, you end up with many distinct nodes that are really the same state, and you're wasting compute evaluating and searching them separately.

Merging child nodes just means recognizing those transpositions, collapsing them into one shared node, and letting the statistics, the value estimates and visit counts, pool together. Technically it stops being a tree and becomes a directed acyclic graph. The payoff is that the search gets more sample efficient, because every rollout that passes through that position contributes to a single estimate instead of being split across duplicates.

The reason I bring it up is less about Go specifically and more as an analogy. When you're thinking about planning in general, whether it's a robot deciding on a sequence of actions or a language model reasoning through steps, there's a lot of redundancy in the space of paths. Many paths converge on the same intermediate state. Learning to recognize "oh, I've effectively been here before" and consolidate is a big part of what makes search tractable. Humans do it constantly; we don't re-derive the world from scratch every time we take a slightly different route to the same situation.

r001.rationale: It says different move sequences can produce the same stones on the board, giving A-then-B versus B-then-A as an example.

astra-6.text:
Imagine two different sequences of moves lead to the same board position. If you represent the search as a tree, those appear as two separate nodes, and you end up exploring the same continuation twice. Instead, you can merge them into one node and share the work you’ve done evaluating what happens next. Technically, you now have a graph rather than a tree.

The caveat in Go is that the board arrangement alone isn’t always enough to establish that two positions are identical. It has to be the same player’s turn, and the relevant history has to agree, because rules like ko can affect which moves are legal.

r001.rationale: It says two different sequences of moves can lead to the same board position.

sol-6.1.text: In a Go search tree, each node represents a board position, and its children represent the positions you could reach by making different moves. Ordinarily, you explore those branches separately. By merging child nodes, I mean recognizing that two branches lead to the same position and letting them share the search you’ve already done. So technically, you end up with a graph rather than a pure tree. The benefit is that you don’t have to rediscover everything about a position just because you reached it through a different sequence of moves.

r001.rationale: It says two branches can lead to the same position, meaning different move sequences reach the same board position.
